title: D major and F major
summary: Build a scale with two sharps and one with a flat, and read all four key signatures.

hook.text: The major scale pattern can start on any note. Press play: this one starts on D, and its [[key-signature|key signature]] shows two sharps. Does it sound like the same bright ladder? How many black keys do you think D needs?

explore.text: Start on D and climb with the pattern: [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[semitone|semitone]], [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[semitone|semitone]]. Then do the same from F. Each time, watch which black keys you need.
explore.goal: Play a major scale from D up to D, then one from F up to F.

cards.text: The pattern from D gives D, E, F♯, G, A, B, C♯, D. That needs two [[sharp|sharps]]: F♯ and C♯. The [[key-signature|key signature]] of D major shows both, F first, then C.

The pattern from F gives F, G, A, B♭, C, D, E, F. A to B would be a [[tone|tone]], but the pattern wants a [[semitone|semitone]], so B is lowered to B♭. F major has one [[flat|flat]], B♭, written on the middle line.

Count the signs to name the key. None is C major. One sharp is G major. Two sharps is D major. One flat is F major. In the bass clef the signs sit on different lines and spaces, but they name the same notes.

alternative.text: Here is a detective trick for sharp keys. Find the last sharp in the [[key-signature|key signature]], then go up to the next letter name. That is the key note. Below, the last sharp is C♯, and the next letter up is D. One flat is always F major.

points: D major has two sharps, F♯ and C♯. Its [[key-signature|key signature]] shows both, F first, then C.
F major has one flat, B♭. Its [[key-signature|key signature]] is a single flat on the middle line.
To name a key from its [[key-signature|key signature]]: no signs is C major, one sharp is G major, two sharps is D major and one flat is F major.
